claims.source: The assembly of the YscDJ ring (Figure 4) revealed that only an elongated arrangement of the C-terminal periplasmic domain of YscD—similar to the X-ray structure—best fits the in situ cryo-ET map, extending up towards the position of the secretin ring.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling and fitting to the cryo-ET map.

claims.claim: An average in situ structure of the Shigella flexneri injectisome was generated at ~7 nm resolution.
claims.source: The structure of an isolated Ysc Yersinia injectisome is not available for comparison; therefore we examined Shigella flexneri bacteria by cryo-ET and generated an average in situ structure of the Shigella flexneri injectisome (Figure 5) at ∼7 nm resolution.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and FSC analysis.

claims.claim: The S. flexneri injectisome has a length measurement between the centers of the membranes of 32 nm.
claims.source: Nevertheless, despite the lower resolution, the map allows to reliably detect the positions of the membrane surrounding the injectisome, resulting in a length measurement between the centers of the membranes of 32 nm (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claims.claim: Full-length YscC was expressed, purified, and reconstituted into liposomes.
claims.source: To evaluate the contribution of the secretin YscC to the elasticity, we expressed and purified full-length YscC, reconstituted it into liposomes, and reconstructed its structure at a resolution of ∼3 nm by cryo-ET and sub-volume averaging (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for studying isolated YscC.

claims.claim: The isolated and liposome-inserted YscC complexes showed several ring densities.
claims.source: The isolated and liposome-inserted YscC complexes showed several ring densities: in the membrane bilayer, ∼5.5 nm below the membrane, and ∼12 nm below the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-ET reconstruction of isolated YscC.

claims.claim: YscC undergoes a 30-40% length extension in the assembled injectisome with respect to its lipid vesicle-reconstituted state.
claims.source: The described assignment of the YscC/YscD junction would correspond to a 30–40% length extension of YscC in the assembled injectisome, with respect to its lipid vesicle-reconstituted state (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparison of in situ and isolated structures.

claims.claim: The Shigella injectisome in situ appeared about 10 nm or ~40% longer than isolated structures.
claims.source: Yersinia injectisomes were found to vary in length by 20% inside the bacterial cells (an intermembrane distance between 30 and 36 nm). Most injectisomes seemed intact; nevertheless, we cannot exclude that under a certain osmotic pressure the injectisomes may detach from the outer membrane. Biophysical experiments would be required to understand, to which limits the basal body may stretch. In addition to the observed length variations, the injectisome's basal bodies were longer in the native context than suggested from single particle structures: the Shigella injectisome in situ appeared about 10 nm or ∼40% longer (32 nm vs 22 nm at the membrane level).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of in situ and isolated structures.

claims.claim: Stretching of YscC by an estimated 5 nm and an elongation of YscD by an estimated 3.5 nm would explain an ~8.5 nm overall extension of the Yersinia injectisome's basal body.
claims.source: Stretching of YscC by an estimated 5 nm and an elongation of YscD by an estimated 3.5 nm would explain an ∼8.5 nm overall extension of the Yersinia injectisome's basal body; the remaining 1.5 nm towards the observed 10 nm elongation of the Shigella system may be attributed to inter-species differences, or the limited resolution of the maps.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural and simulation data.

claims.claim: The isolated S. flexneri injectisome would have to be stretched by ~40% to match the dimensions of the average in situ Yersinia structure.
claims.source: Even the shortest of our MRA class averages of in situ Yersinia injectisomes (Figure 2B) is still longer than the isolated Shigella injectisome, which would have to be stretched by ∼40% to match the dimensions of the average in situ Yersinia structure (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of structures shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes show high overall similarity.
claims.source: The in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes show high overall similarity considering the lower resolution of the Shigella injectisome: the overall dimensions, ring hierarchy and the peptidoglycan attachment location are conserved.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of the two in situ structures.

claims.claim: In the Yersinia injectisome, the torus ring assigned to YscV was ~5 nm below the membrane.
claims.source: We could detect a significant difference in the location of the torus ring assigned to the N-terminus or YscV/MxiA (Abrusci et al., 2013). In the Yersinia injectisome, it was ∼5 nm below the membrane, while in the Shigella injectisome it was ∼10 nm below the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the reconstruction.

claims.claim: In the Shigella injectisome, the torus ring assigned to MxiA was ~10 nm below the membrane.
claims.source: We could detect a significant difference in the location of the torus ring assigned to the N-terminus or YscV/MxiA (Abrusci et al., 2013). In the Yersinia injectisome, it was ∼5 nm below the membrane, while in the Shigella injectisome it was ∼10 nm below the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the reconstruction.

claims.claim: The in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes did not reveal obvious C-rings.
claims.source: Injectisomes contain proteins homologous to FliN and FliM, termed YscQ in Yersinia and Spa33 in Shigella, which are suggested to form a C-ring (Morita-Ishihara et al., 2006) similar to bacterial flagellar motors. However, the in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes did not reveal obvious C-rings (Figure 2A,B and Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstructions.

claims.claim: YscQ could be unstructured or only transiently associated with the injectisome.
claims.source: This could be caused by YscQ being unstructured, or being only transiently associated with the injectisome.
claims.evidence: This is speculation to explain the absence of visible C-rings.

claims.claim: Exposure of Y. enterocolitica bacteria to osmotic stress from high salt conditions resulted in a significant elongation of their basal bodies.
claims.source: In order to influence the intermembrane distance, we placed Y. enterocolitica bacteria in high salt media (10-fold concentrated PBS; 10× PBS). The osmotic pressure experienced by the bacterial membranes (Koch, 1998) significantly widened the periplasmic space, while injectisomes remained in place and were studied by cryo-ET. The length of observed basal bodies increased by ∼10% (with statistical significance, Figure 7), while preserving the basal bodies seemingly intact.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Bacteria are likely exposed to considerable physical forces in vivo.
claims.source: Bacteria are likely exposed to considerable physical forces in vivo, originating from swimming motions, contact with host cells, or from changes in osmolarity of the surrounding medium.
claims.evidence: This is general knowledge about bacterial physiology.

claims.claim: The observed elasticity might allow the injectisome to better cope with membrane stresses.
claims.source: We hypothesize that the here observed elasticity might allow the injectisome to better cope with such membrane stresses.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed flexibility and osmotic stress experiments.

claims.claim: The significantly larger basal bodies of flagellar motors do not vary in length.
claims.source: Recently, it was suggested that injectisomes may rotate upon action (Ohgita et al., 2013), similarly to the evolutionary related flagellar motors. To our knowledge, however, the significantly larger basal bodies of flagellar motors do not vary in length, despite their active rotation.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of flagellar motor structures from the literature.

claims.claim: The basal bodies of the bacterial flagellar motors do not seem to differ in dimensions between their isolated and in situ structures.
claims.source: Furthermore, the basal bodies of the bacterial flagellar motors do not seem to differ in dimensions between their isolated and in situ structures (Chen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on flagellar motors.

claims.claim: For more fragile protein complexes that span two membranes, tertiary structure elasticity may constitute a general mechanism for structural protection.
claims.source: We here hypothesize that for more fragile protein complexes that span two membranes, tertiary structure elasticity may constitute a general mechanism for structural protection.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings in this study.

claims.claim: The channel of the injectisome's needle is resolved at the OM.
claims.source: The channel of the injectisome's needle is resolved at the OM.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claims.claim: A large ring-like structure can be discerned on the cytoplasmic side of the IM.
claims.source: Further, a large ring-like structure can be discerned on the cytoplasmic side of the IM (Figure 2A, yellow).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstruction shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A smaller, torus-like structure is localized ~5 nm underneath the membrane, which is tentatively proposed to be the export gate YscV.
claims.source: It surrounds a smaller, torus-like structure localized ∼5 nm underneath the membrane, which we tentatively propose to be the export gate YscV (Figure 2A, red), based on the localization of the export gate protein FlhA of the flagella motor (Abrusci et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to the flagellar motor system.

claims.claim: The density below the export gate likely corresponds to the YscN ATPase.
claims.source: Similarly, in analogy to the flagellar motor system (Chen et al., 2011), the density below the export gate likely corresponds to the YscN ATPase.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to the flagellar motor system.

claims.claim: The YscC-D junction is distinguishable in the density map.
claims.source: The YscC-D junction is distinguishable in the density map and indicated in the density assignment (Figure 2A, asterisk).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claims.claim: Most of the YscD/YscJ interactions occur between the first periplasmic domain of YscD and the C-terminal domain of YscJ.
claims.source: Most of the YscD/YscJ interactions occur between the first periplasmic domain of YscD and the C-terminal domain of YscJ.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the molecular modeling and assembly.

claims.claim: The 24-meric YscD assembly is compatible with the basal body's diameter as observed by cryo-EM.
claims.source: In particular, the 24-meric YscD assembly is compatible with the basal body's diameter, as observed by cryo-EM, while a higher number of YscD units would lead to a poorer match with the experimental data.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling and fitting to the cryo-ET map.

claims.claim: The model constructed of 24 YscJ molecules does not produce gaps or overlaps in the final structural assembly.
claims.source: Taking the observed stoichiometry of EscJ into account (Crepin et al., 2005; Yip et al., 2005), the model constructed of 24 YscJ molecules does not produce gaps or overlaps in the final structural assembly, as we otherwise obtained when using a higher or lower stoichiometry.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and citations to EscJ stoichiometry.

claims.claim: MD simulations suggested a limited fluctuation for the TM portion of YscD embedded in a membrane model.
claims.source: MD simulations also suggested a limited fluctuation for this portion of YscD embedded in a membrane model, confirming the preferential orientation found in the 24-mer YscD ring assembly (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claims.claim: The cryo-ET density could be optimally fitted only by extended forms similar to the X-ray YscD conformation.
claims.source: Although the cryo-ET density could be optimally fitted only by extended forms similar to the X-ray YscD conformation, MD snapshots of individual monomers in more compact forms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) allowed the construction, without incurring in steric clashes, of YscD 24-mer ring structures representative of possible states of intermediate compression compared to the fully extended ring model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling and fitting to the cryo-ET map.

results.result: The authors present the first three-dimensional structures of Yersinia enterocolitica and Shigella flexneri injectisomes in situ, representing the first structural analysis of the Yersinia injectisome.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 are well-supported by cryo-ET experimental data at ~4 nm resolution for Y. enterocolitica and ~7 nm for S. flexneri. The novelty claims are substantiated by the absence of prior in situ structures for these systems and the detailed structural reconstructions presented.

results.result: Basal bodies of injectisomes inside bacterial cells show length variations of 20%, with intermembrane distances ranging from 30 to 36 nm, indicating high flexibility in the cellular context.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C33, and C34 are supported by MRA classification data showing intermembrane distance variations from 30-36 nm. The 20% variation is directly measured and the flexibility inference is reasonable given the observed structural heterogeneity.

results.result: In situ structures of Y. enterocolitica and S. flexneri injectisomes have similar dimensions (~32-33 nm intermembrane distance) and are significantly longer (~10 nm or ~40%) than isolated structures of related injectisomes from Salmonella and Shigella.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C28-C29, C49, and C53 are well-supported by direct measurements from cryo-ET reconstructions and comparisons with published isolated structures. The ~10 nm difference is consistently observed across multiple comparisons, and CEMOVIS imaging (C30) independently confirms the intermembrane distances.

results.result: The crystal structure of YscD shows an elongated conformation with three linearly arranged domains, each comprising an αββαβ-ring building motif, which is extended compared to the homologous PrgH protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C35-C37 are supported by X-ray crystallography data at 2.7 Å resolution for wild-type and 1.4 Å for G283P mutant. The structural comparison with PrgH is valid and the domain architecture is clearly defined.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that YscD exhibits elongation elasticity through tertiary structure rearrangement, with the hinge between domains 2 and 3 (residues A282-N284) being primarily responsible for flexibility. YscD can undergo maximal elongation of ~3.5 nm while opposing stretching with forces of 35±15 pN per monomer.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C38, C42-C45 are supported by extensive MD simulations including steered MD showing barrier-free transitions between compact and extended conformations. The force measurements and elongation distances are quantitatively determined from simulations and are comparable to other elastic proteins.

results.result: The secretin YscC at the outer membrane is stretched by 30-40% in situ compared to its isolated liposome-embedded conformation, as determined by comparing in situ cryo-ET structures with isolated YscC reconstituted in liposomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C50-C52 are supported by direct comparison of cryo-ET reconstructions of isolated YscC in liposomes (~3 nm resolution) with the in situ structure. The 30-40% extension is inferred from structural measurements and junction assignments, though some uncertainty exists in the exact YscC-YscD junction location.

results.result: A pseudo-atomic model of the YscDJ inner membrane ring was constructed using integrative modeling combining cryo-ET data, X-ray structures, cross-linking restraints, and MD simulations. The model reveals a 24-meric assembly where only elongated YscD conformations fit the in situ cryo-ET map.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47, C72-C74, C76-C77 are supported by the integrative modeling approach using particle swarm optimization with multiple experimental restraints. The 24-mer stoichiometry is consistent with homologous systems and produces no gaps or overlaps. However, the limited resolution of cryo-ET (~4 nm) means the model represents one plausible interpretation.

results.result: The G283P mutation in YscD results in a more rigid but still functional protein, as demonstrated by secretion assays and crystallographic B-factor analysis showing lower atomic mobility while maintaining type III secretion activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by functional secretion assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and high-resolution crystal structure (1.4 Å) showing reduced B-factors. The mutation successfully stabilized the protein for better crystallography while preserving biological function.

results.result: The combined stretching of YscC (~5 nm) and elongation of YscD (~3.5 nm) accounts for ~8.5 nm of the observed ~10 nm extension in the Yersinia injectisome basal body, with the remaining 1.5 nm attributed to inter-species differences or resolution limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by combining structural measurements and simulation data. The calculation is internally consistent and accounts for most of the observed elongation. The acknowledgment of remaining uncertainty (1.5 nm) is appropriate given the resolution limitations.

results.result: Exposure of Y. enterocolitica bacteria to osmotic stress from high salt conditions (10× PBS) resulted in a statistically significant ~10% elongation of injectisome basal bodies while preserving structural integrity.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by cryo-ET data with statistical analysis (Figure 7) showing significant differences (p=0.05 and p=0.02) between conditions. This provides experimental validation of the elasticity hypothesis under physiological stress conditions.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that elasticity is critical for two-membrane spanning protein complexes to cope with variations in intermembrane distance and may constitute a general mechanism for structural protection in fragile complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C63, and C66 represent hypotheses based on the observed flexibility and osmotic stress experiments. While the data support the existence of elasticity, the functional importance and generality to other systems remain speculative. Direct functional tests linking elasticity to biological fitness or survival under stress are not provided.

results.result: Cryo-electron tomography was applied to visualize injectisomes in intact Y. enterocolitica cells, including genetically engineered minicells with reduced thickness, yielding a reconstruction at ~4 nm resolution using sub-tomogram averaging with customized alignment strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C25-C27 describe the methodological approach and are well-supported by detailed methods, FSC analysis showing ~4 nm resolution, and validation through multiple imaging approaches including focal pair tomography and CEMOVIS.

results.result: CEMOVIS imaging independently confirmed the intermembrane distance measurements obtained from plunge-frozen samples.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by independent measurements using CEMOVIS showing similar intermembrane distance distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), validating that the plunge-freezing method did not introduce artifacts in membrane spacing.

results.result: In situ reconstructions of Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes show high overall similarity in dimensions, ring hierarchy, and peptidoglycan attachment, but differ in the location of the torus ring assigned to YscV/MxiA (~5 nm vs ~10 nm below the membrane).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by direct comparison of the two in situ structures. The overall similarity is evident despite lower resolution for Shigella (~7 nm), and the difference in YscV/MxiA location is a specific, measurable distinction between the two systems.

results.result: The in situ reconstructions did not reveal obvious C-rings, which could be due to YscQ being unstructured or only transiently associated with the injectisome.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is a valid observation from the cryo-ET data, but C60 is speculation. The absence of visible C-rings could have multiple explanations including structural disorder, transient association, or resolution limitations. No additional experiments were performed to distinguish between these possibilities.

results.result: Flagellar motor basal bodies, which are evolutionarily related to injectisomes, do not show length variations or dimensional differences between isolated and in situ structures, contrasting with the observed injectisome flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by citations to published flagellar motor structures. This comparison strengthens the argument that injectisome elasticity may be functionally distinct from the more rigid flagellar motors, though the functional significance remains speculative.

results.result: Background information on injectisomes including their function, composition, phylogenetic classification, structural organization, and evolutionary relationship to flagellar motors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C22 represent established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These provide necessary context for the novel findings but are not original results of this study.

results.result: Variations in injectisome appearance observed by cryo-ET indicate intrinsic flexibility of the structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 is a reasonable inference from the observed structural variations documented in the cryo-ET data. The inference is strengthened by subsequent quantitative MRA analysis showing the range of conformations.

results.result: Detailed structural measurements and component assignments in the average injectisome structure, including lateral diameters, ring structures, and tentative identification of cytoplasmic components based on analogy to flagellar motors.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32, C67-C71 represent direct measurements and component assignments from the cryo-ET reconstruction. The measurements are well-supported, though assignments of cytoplasmic components (C69-C70) are tentative inferences based on homology to flagellar motors rather than direct identification.

results.result: An average in situ structure of the Shigella flexneri injectisome was generated at ~7 nm resolution to enable comparison with the Yersinia structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by cryo-ET data and FSC analysis. The lower resolution compared to Yersinia (~7 nm vs ~4 nm) is acknowledged and attributed to the extreme thickness of S. flexneri bacteria, which is a reasonable technical limitation.

results.result: Bacteria are likely exposed to considerable physical forces in vivo from swimming motions, host cell contact, and osmolarity changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 represents general knowledge about bacterial physiology and provides context for the functional significance of the observed elasticity. This is well-established background information.

results.result: The authors present the first in situ three-dimensional structures of Yersinia enterocolitica and Shigella flexneri injectisomes obtained by cryo-electron tomography. They engineered Y. enterocolitica minicells to improve imaging quality and achieved a reconstruction at ~4 nm resolution using sub-tomogram averaging with a customized local feature alignment strategy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed concern about potential over-alignment artifacts in the sub-tomogram averaging structures, particularly noting 'disconnected and inverted densities' in some figures. They requested validation through independent alignment of dataset halves or proper low-pass filtering to rule out artifacts, indicating the structural claims require additional methodological verification before full acceptance.

results.result: The authors report that injectisome basal bodies show 20% length variations in situ, with intermembrane distances ranging from 30 to 36 nm (average ~33 nm). This is significantly larger than the ~20 nm expected from isolated structures and was confirmed by independent CEMOVIS imaging, suggesting high flexibility of the basal body in the cellular context.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found the length variation results 'interesting and unexpected,' they raised concerns about potential artifacts from the alignment methodology. The 'substantial differences in structure dependent on the mask used in Figure 2B' were specifically noted as potentially problematic, requiring additional validation before these flexibility claims can be fully supported.

results.result: The in situ structures of Y. enterocolitica and S. flexneri injectisomes had similar dimensions (~32-33 nm intermembrane distance) and were significantly longer (~10 nm or ~40% longer) than isolated structures of related injectisomes from Salmonella and Shigella. The two in situ reconstructions show high overall similarity in dimensions, ring hierarchy, and peptidoglycan attachment location.
results.evaluation: Reviewers were positive about the 'interesting' comparison between in vitro and in situ results, but the methodological concerns about over-alignment artifacts apply equally to these comparative measurements. The reliability of the dimensional differences between in situ and isolated structures depends on resolving the technical concerns about the averaging procedures.

results.result: The crystal structure of YscD150-362 at 2.7 Å resolution showed three linearly arranged domains with an extended conformation compared to the homologous PrgH protein. MD simulations revealed that the connecting hinge (residues A282-N284) between the second and third periplasmic domains is mainly responsible for YscD's high flexibility. The G283P mutant showed a slightly more bent but still functional structure with lower B-factors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the crystallographic data or the structural characterization of YscD. The crystal structures and MD simulations appear to be accepted as presented, with no methodological critiques directed at these specific findings.

results.result: YscD appeared elongated compared to homologous PrgH, and molecular dynamics simulations documented its elongation elasticity. MD simulations showed both straight and bent structures are stable conformational states, with stretching forces producing an almost barrier-free transition from compact to extended conformation. The periplasmic domains can undergo maximal elongation of about 3.5 nm (50% elongation) while opposing stretching with only 35 ± 15 pN per monomer.
results.evaluation: The MD simulation results were not questioned by reviewers. These computational findings about YscD flexibility and elasticity appear to be accepted as valid supporting evidence for the structural interpretations.

results.result: The G283P mutation in YscD resulted in a protein that was still functional for type III secretion in vivo, as demonstrated by secretion assays.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the functional validation experiments. This supporting biochemical evidence appears to be accepted without critique.

results.result: A pseudo-atomic model of the inner membrane part of the basal body was constructed by combining experimental data with molecular modeling and simulations. The assembly revealed that only an elongated arrangement of YscD's C-terminal periplasmic domain best fits the in situ cryo-ET map. The 24-meric YscD assembly is compatible with the basal body's diameter, and the model with 24 YscJ molecules produces no gaps or overlaps.
results.evaluation: The modeling and fitting results depend on the reliability of the underlying cryo-ET density maps. Since reviewers raised concerns about potential over-alignment artifacts in the sub-tomogram averaging structures, the quality of the fitting and the conclusions about the elongated YscD conformation require validation of the density maps before these modeling results can be fully supported.

results.result: The secretin YscC was expressed, purified, and reconstituted into liposomes for structural analysis. Comparison of isolated YscC with the in situ structure suggests YscC undergoes 30-40% length extension in the assembled injectisome. Combined with YscD elongation of 3.5 nm, this would explain ~8.5 nm of the observed overall extension.
results.evaluation: Reviewers specifically noted that the YscC structure in liposomes (Figure 6B) shows 'disconnected and inverted densities' which are 'a particular concern' and could result from over-alignment artifacts. This directly challenges the reliability of the YscC structural comparison and the inferred stretching calculations.

results.result: The authors assigned specific densities to injectisome components: a torus-like structure ~5 nm below the membrane in Yersinia (tentatively YscV export gate) and ~10 nm below in Shigella (MxiA), with density below likely corresponding to YscN ATPase. However, no obvious C-rings were observed in either reconstruction, though YscQ/Spa33 proteins are expected to form such structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated that 'the position of YscV can be interpreted only after these tests' referring to the requested validation of alignment procedures. The density assignments and component localizations depend on the reliability of the sub-tomogram averaging, which requires methodological validation.

results.result: Exposure of Y. enterocolitica bacteria to osmotic stress from high salt conditions (10× PBS) resulted in significant elongation of basal bodies by ~10%, while preserving the structures seemingly intact.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about the osmotic stress experiments. These functional validation experiments appear to be accepted as supporting evidence for the elasticity hypothesis.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that elasticity is critical for two-membrane spanning protein complexes to cope with variations in intermembrane distance and membrane stresses, and may constitute a general mechanism for structural protection of fragile complexes.
results.evaluation: This interpretive hypothesis depends on the validity of the underlying structural observations of flexibility and elongation. Since reviewers questioned the reliability of the structural measurements due to potential alignment artifacts, the broader hypothesis about elasticity as a protective mechanism remains uncertain until the technical concerns are resolved.

results.result: Background claims about injectisome structure, function, composition, and evolutionary relationships, including comparisons with flagellar motors and general knowledge about bacterial physiology and forces.
results.evaluation: These are established background facts from the literature that reviewers did not question. They provide context for the novel findings.

results.result: Various observational claims about injectisome features including variations indicating flexibility, dimensional measurements, absence of C-rings, and identification of structural features like the needle channel and ring-like structures.
results.evaluation: These observational claims are derived from the cryo-ET reconstructions and are subject to the same methodological concerns about over-alignment artifacts raised by reviewers. Their reliability depends on validation of the averaging procedures.

comparisons.comparison: Both address claims C2-C4 about cryo-ET structures. OpenEval finds them well-supported by experimental data, while peer reviewers express concern about potential over-alignment artifacts and disconnected densities, requesting additional validation. This represents a significant disagreement on data quality.

Both evaluate claims C5, C33-C34 about intermembrane distance variations and flexibility. OpenEval finds the claims supported by MRA classification data, while peer reviewers find the results 'interesting' but raise concerns about alignment artifacts and mask-dependent structural differences, marking them as uncertain.

Both address claims C6-C7, C28-C29, C49, C53 about dimensional differences between in situ and isolated structures. OpenEval finds these well-supported by direct measurements, while peer reviewers find the comparison 'interesting' but uncertain due to methodological concerns about over-alignment artifacts.

Both evaluate claims C8, C35-C37 about YscD crystallography. OpenEval finds them supported by high-resolution X-ray data, and peer reviewers also accept these findings without raising concerns. This represents strong agreement.

Both address claims C9, C42-C45 about MD simulations of YscD flexibility. OpenEval finds them supported by extensive simulation data, and peer reviewers also accept these computational findings without critique. This represents agreement on the simulation results.

Both evaluate claims C10, C50-C52 about YscC extension. OpenEval finds them supported by cryo-ET comparisons with some uncertainty about junction location, while peer reviewers specifically note 'disconnected and inverted densities' in the YscC liposome structure as a particular concern, marking it uncertain.

Both address claims C46-C47, C72-C74, C76-C77 about integrative modeling and stoichiometry. OpenEval finds them supported while acknowledging resolution limitations, while peer reviewers mark them uncertain because the modeling depends on potentially artifact-affected density maps.

Both evaluate claims C39-C41 about the G283P mutation. OpenEval finds them supported by functional assays and crystal structure, and peer reviewers accept the functional validation without concerns. This represents agreement.

OpenEval evaluates claims C54-C55 about elongation calculations as supported, while peer reviewers' concerns about YscC structural artifacts (R8) directly impact the reliability of these calculations, though C54 is only partially overlapping with peer R8.

Both evaluate claim C61 about osmotic stress experiments. OpenEval finds it supported by cryo-ET data with statistical significance, and peer reviewers accept these functional validation experiments without concerns. This represents agreement.

Both address claims C11, C63, C66 about the elasticity hypothesis. OpenEval marks them uncertain due to lack of direct functional tests, while peer reviewers also mark them uncertain because the hypothesis depends on structural observations that require methodological validation. Both agree on uncertainty but for different reasons.

OpenEval R12 addresses methodological claims C23, C25-C27 as supported, while peer R1 includes these same claims but expresses concern about the methodology, specifically requesting validation of alignment procedures. This represents disagreement on methodological rigor.

OpenEval evaluates claim C30 (CEMOVIS validation) as supported, while peer R2 includes C30 among claims marked uncertain due to alignment concerns. OpenEval views CEMOVIS as independent validation, while peer reviewers remain concerned about artifacts.

Both address claims C56-C58 about comparison between Yersinia and Shigella structures. OpenEval finds them supported despite lower Shigella resolution, while peer reviewers mark them uncertain, explicitly stating that component positions like YscV require validation of alignment procedures first.

Both evaluate claims C59-C60 about C-ring absence. OpenEval marks C60 as uncertain speculation, while peer R9 includes C59 among claims requiring methodological validation. Both agree on uncertainty but OpenEval distinguishes observation (C59) from interpretation (C60).
